name: Mahāvihāra fraternity (Mahāvihāra-vāsins)

tradition.text: founded with the Great Monastery given to Mahinda by King Devānampiya Tissa (3rd c. BCE); sole recognized fraternity after Parakkamabāhu I's unification

scholarly.text: 3rd c. BCE – 1165 CE as a separate fraternity; its commentarial orthodoxy continues in all modern Theravāda

transmissions_given.what: the Pali commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) and the Visuddhimagga as the orthodox exegesis of the canon; Sri Lankan ordination lineages sent to Burma and Thailand

distinctive_positions: The Pali Tipiṭaka including the seven Abhidhamma books is the Buddha's word; the Sinhala commentaries (rendered into Pali by Buddhaghosa and others) are the authoritative explanation.
Rejection of the Vetulya (Vaitulya) texts accepted at the Abhayagiri as not the Buddha's word.
The path as the seven purifications and the forty meditation subjects as systematized in the Visuddhimagga.
summary: The fraternity of the Great Monastery at Anurādhapura, whose commentarial tradition Buddhaghosa rendered into Pali in the 5th century and which, after the 12th-century unification of the Sri Lankan saṅgha, became the normative Theravāda.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U37 for the commentarial orthodoxy; parent lin:theravada (owned by U36). The rival fraternities were the Abhayagiri and (later) the Jetavana.

name: Abhayagiri fraternity (Abhayagiri-vāsins)

tradition.text: founded when King Vaṭṭagāmaṇī Abhaya built the Abhayagiri monastery (1st c. BCE, per the Mahāvaṃsa); absorbed in the 12th-c. unification

distinctive_positions: Reported (by the Mahāvihāra chronicles) to have accepted the Vetulya texts and to have had contacts with Mahāyāna teachers.
The Vimuttimagga is associated with this fraternity by some scholars (a scholarly hypothesis, not a tradition's claim).
summary: The rival Sri Lankan fraternity to the Mahāvihāra, known mainly through Mahāvihāra chronicles and foreign reports; its own literature is largely lost, which is why the Mahāvihāra commentaries became the Theravāda norm.
notes: Known largely through the reports of its rivals (Mahāvaṃsa, Cūḷavaṃsa) — treat characterizations as reported by opponents. Created by U37.

name: Ledi Sayadaw tradition

tradition.text: Ledi Sayadaw began teaching insight to monks and laypeople at the Ledi forest monastery near Monywa from the 1880s

transmissions_received.what: the Abhidhamma and commentarial tradition as studied in Burma
transmissions_received.evidence: Ledi's Pali and Burmese manuals on the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha

transmissions_given.what: the lay insight practice passed through Saya Thetgyi to U Ba Khin

distinctive_positions: Laypeople as well as monks should study the Abhidhamma and practise insight now, because the time of the Buddha's dispensation in which liberation is possible is limited.
Mindfulness of breathing (or other calm) as a base, then insight into the four elements, feeling and the aggregates, may be enough for liberation without full absorption (the 'dry-insight' vehicle).
Critical re-examination of the Abhidhamma sub-commentaries (the Paramatthadīpanī's critique of the Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī).
The thirty-seven requisites of awakening must be developed; merely wishing for a future birth with a Buddha is unwise.
summary: Lineage stemming from the Burmese scholar-monk Ledi Sayadaw (1846–1923), who wrote a series of Pali and Burmese manuals (dīpanī) and made the Abhidhamma and insight meditation accessible to laypeople; the root of the U Ba Khin – Goenka tradition.

name: U Ba Khin – S. N. Goenka tradition (Sayagyi U Ba Khin lineage)

tradition.text: the tradition's account: the technique was preserved in its purity in Burma by a chain of teachers from the Buddha's time (via the missionaries Soṇa and Uttara to Suvaṇṇabhūmi) and revived by Ledi Sayadaw; U Ba Khin founded the IMC in 1952; Goenka began teaching in India in 1969

scholarly.text: IMC Yangon 1952; Goenka's courses from 1969; Dhamma Giri 1976

transmissions_received.what: the practice of observing sensations (vedanā) with awareness of impermanence, via Saya Thetgyi

distinctive_positions: A ten-day residential course: five precepts (sīla), mindfulness of respiration at the nostrils (samādhi) for the first days, then insight by systematic observation of bodily sensations with equanimity (paññā), ending with loving-kindness (mettā).
Reacting to sensations with craving or aversion multiplies saṅkhāras; equanimous observation of sensations as impermanent eradicates them.
The teaching is presented as non-sectarian and universal; courses are given free, supported by donations of past students.
U Ba Khin: 'the clock of vipassanā has struck' — the revival of the practice 2,500 years after the Buddha (the tradition's account).
summary: The lay insight lineage of Saya Thetgyi, Sayagyi U Ba Khin (1899–1971) and S. N. Goenka (1924–2013), whose standardized ten-day courses of mindfulness of respiration and body-scanning insight spread from Burma and India worldwide.

name: Mahāsi Sayadaw tradition (the 'new Burmese method')

tradition.text: Mahāsi Sayadaw taught at Mahāsi monastery (Seikkhun) from 1938 and at the Sāsana Yeiktha in Rangoon from 1949

transmissions_received.what: the satipaṭṭhāna practice as taught by Mingun Jetavana Sayadaw
transmissions_received.evidence: Mahāsi's own acknowledgement of his teacher

distinctive_positions: Bare, moment-to-moment noting of whatever arises — beginning with the rising and falling of the abdomen and extending to all sensations, thoughts and actions — develops momentary concentration (khaṇika-samādhi) sufficient for insight without prior absorption (the vipassanā-yānika or dry-insight vehicle).
Intensive retreat with alternating sitting and walking, continuous noting in daily activities and regular interviews with the teacher.
The meditator passes through the insight knowledges in the order described in the Visuddhimagga and Paṭisambhidāmagga, which Mahāsi described from practice in The Progress of Insight.
summary: The intensive insight method of Mahāsi Sayadaw (1904–1982), based on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta and the Visuddhimagga's insight knowledges, taught at the Sāsana Yeiktha from 1949 and spread across Theravāda Asia and to the West.

name: Sunlun Sayadaw tradition
regions: Burma (Sunlun monastery, Myingyan; Sunlun Gu Kyaung, Yangon)

tradition.text: founded by the formerly unlettered farmer-monk Sunlun Sayadaw (U Kawi) after his own attainment in the 1920s

distinctive_positions: Vigorous, strong breathing at the start of a sitting to build concentration quickly, followed by unmoving attention to the sensation of touch (at the nostrils and then throughout the body).
Painful feeling is not avoided: the meditator sits without moving and watches pain with great energy until it breaks up — effort (viriya) is emphasized.
Practice without reliance on scriptural learning; mindfulness of touch as the direct way.
summary: A Burmese insight lineage from Sunlun Sayadaw (U Kawi, 1878–1952), known for its strong-breathing opening and its unflinching mindfulness of touch and painful sensation.
notes: Method summary only; no breath counts or durations recorded. Dates of founding approximate.

name: Pa-Auk tradition (Pa-Auk Tawya)
regions: branches in Asia and the West

tradition.text: Pa-Auk Sayadaw (Āciṇṇa, b. 1934) became abbot of Pa-Auk Tawya in 1981

distinctive_positions: Close adherence to the Visuddhimagga and Abhidhamma as a practical manual.

Samatha-first route: mindfulness of breathing to the fourth jhāna with a bright counterpart sign, then the kasiṇas, the formless attainments and the immeasurables; or, for the pure-insight vehicle, four-elements meditation to access concentration.

Insight requires seeing ultimate realities directly: the tiny material groups (rūpa-kalāpa) and their elements, the mind-moments of cognitive processes with their mental factors, and dependent origination across past and future lives, before contemplating the three characteristics.
summary: The Burmese forest tradition of Pa-Auk Sayadaw (b. 1934), which teaches the Visuddhimagga's full sequence of calm and insight, including direct discernment of Abhidhamma ultimate realities.

name: Thai Forest tradition (Kammaṭṭhāna forest tradition)
regions: the West (Wat Pah Nanachat, Amaravati, Metta Forest Monastery, etc.)

tradition.text: Ajahn Sao and Ajahn Mun took up the ascetic wandering life (dhutaṅga) in the forests of Isan from the late 19th/early 20th century; the tradition regards it as a return to the practice of the Buddha's time

scholarly.text: c. 1900 onward, within the Dhammayut order and later also the Mahānikāya

transmissions_received.what: the reformed Vinaya discipline and ordination of the Dhammayut order
transmissions_received.evidence: Ajahn Sao and Ajahn Mun were Dhammayut monks

distinctive_positions: Strict observance of the Vinaya and the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga): forest dwelling, alms-round, one meal a day, wandering (tudong) in wilderness and charnel places.

Meditation with the parikamma word 'buddho' and on the breath, and contemplation of the body (its thirty-two parts, foulness, elements) until the mind converges in calm and sees the body's true nature.
Calm and insight developed together; direct experience in the heart (citta) is valued over textual learning, though the teachers used the Pali terms.
The mind in itself is radiant; defilements are visitors (āgantuka) — with the later teaching (Ajahn Maha Boowa) that even the radiant citta must be seen through, since ignorance can dwell in it.
The tradition's biographies record visions, signs and the teachers' attainments (the tradition's account).
summary: The Thai forest meditation lineage descending from Ajahn Sao Kantasīlo (1861–1941) and Ajahn Mun Bhūridatta (1870–1949), emphasizing Vinaya, dhutaṅga austerities, 'buddho' and body contemplation, and realization in the heart; spread internationally through Ajahn Chah's and Ajahn Lee's lines.

name: Suan Mokkh (Buddhadāsa's tradition)
distinctive_positions: Return to the Buddha's words (the suttas) over later commentarial layers; the essential teaching is the emptying of 'I' and 'mine' (tua-ku khong-ku).
Dependent origination describes the arising of suffering and of the 'self' within a single sequence of sense-contact in present experience, not only across three lives.
'Birth' in its Dhamma-language sense is the birth of the ego-sense; nibbāna is the coolness of the extinction of defilements here and now.
Everyday language and Dhamma language (phasa khon, phasa tham) must be distinguished.
Mindfulness with breathing in its sixteen steps as a complete path; work done with a mind void of self (chit wang).
summary: The reformist Thai tradition of Buddhadāsa Bhikkhu (1906–1993) and his forest monastery Suan Mokkh, teaching emptiness of self, present-moment dependent origination and the sixteen-step mindfulness with breathing.

name: Borān kammaṭṭhāna (old meditation; the yogāvacara tradition)

tradition.text: presented in its manuals as the Buddha's own method handed down by yogāvacaras; brought to Kandy with the Siamese ordination mission of 1753 (the tradition's account)

scholarly.text: attested in manuscripts from at least the 17th–18th c.; probably older; marginalized by the 19th–20th c. reforms

transmissions_given.what: the placing of meditative objects at bodily locations and syllable recitation (scholarly hypothesis of continuity)

distinctive_positions: Meditation proceeds by installing meditative qualities (the five kinds of rapture, the tranquillities, etc.) at specific points of the body in a fixed order, using Pali syllables and recitations.
Symbolic correspondences between the stages of meditation, embryology, the letters of the Pali alphabet and the Abhidhamma lists.
Teaching was given by a teacher to a qualified pupil after preliminary rites (offerings, requesting the meditation subject).
summary: The pre-reform meditation system of mainland Southeast Asian and Sri Lankan Theravāda, known from manuals such as the Yogāvacara's Manual, which uses bodily placement, syllables and ritual; largely displaced by the 19th–20th-century reforms and now studied and partly revived.
notes: Low confidence throughout: the tradition is known through a few published manuscripts and recent scholarship; its practices are recorded here in summary only. 'Tantric Theravāda' is a contested scholars' label, not the tradition's own.

name: Dhammakāya meditation tradition (Vijjā Dhammakāya; Wat Paknam)
regions: Bangkok (Wat Paknam Bhasicharoen; Wat Phra Dhammakaya, Pathum Thani)

tradition.text: Luang Pu Sodh Candasaro rediscovered the Dhammakāya knowledge in 1917 (the tradition's account: the method had been lost some 500 years after the Buddha)

transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly hypothesis of continuity with borān kammaṭṭhāna

distinctive_positions: The mind is brought to rest at the centre of the body (the seventh base, two finger-breadths above the navel) while visualizing a bright crystal sphere and reciting 'sammā arahaṃ'.
Successive refined inner bodies appear, culminating in the Dhammakāya, the Buddha-body within.
Nibbāna is described as a true self (attā) — a teaching contested by other Thai Theravāda scholars.
summary: The Thai meditation tradition founded by Luang Pu Sodh Candasaro (1884–1959) of Wat Paknam, teaching concentration at the body's centre leading to the inner Dhammakāya; continued by Wat Paknam and by the Wat Phra Dhammakaya movement.

name: Mogok Sayadaw tradition
distinctive_positions: Understanding dependent origination (taught with a chart) is the foundation for insight.
Contemplation of mind and feeling: seeing each arising consciousness and feeling vanish (seeing arising and passing away) as the direct road to the path.
summary: Burmese insight lineage of Mogok Sayadaw (U Vimala, 1899–1962), stressing an intellectual grasp of dependent origination followed by contemplation of the arising and passing of mind and feeling.
notes: Low confidence on details; no digitized texts of this tradition located.

name: Dhammayuttika Nikāya (Dhammayut order)

tradition.text: founded by the monk-prince Vajirañāṇa (later King Mongkut) in the 1830s

transmissions_given.what: strict Vinaya discipline; the early forest masters were Dhammayut

distinctive_positions: Reform of monastic discipline according to the Pali Vinaya (as read by the reformers), with a renewed Mon ordination lineage.
Emphasis on Pali textual study and suspicion of practices not found in the canon (a factor in the decline of borān kammaṭṭhāna).
summary: The reformist Thai monastic order founded by Vajirañāṇa (King Mongkut) in the 1830s; the order of the early Thai Forest masters.

name: Andhakas (as named in the Kathāvatthu commentary)
distinctive_positions: Reported (by the Kathāvatthu commentary) to hold, among others, that an arahant can be defiled by emissions induced by deities, can have ignorance and doubt, and can be instructed by others.
Reported to hold that the four truths are penetrated gradually.
summary: A group of Mahāsāṅghika-derived schools of the Andhra region to which the Kathāvatthu commentary attributes many of the views refuted in the Kathāvatthu.
notes: Known here only through the Theravāda commentary (reported by an opponent). Created by U37 to name the opponents of Kathāvatthu debates; U38 owns lin:mahasanghika.

name: Uttarāpathakas ('Northerners', as named in the Kathāvatthu commentary)
distinctive_positions: Reported (by the Kathāvatthu commentary) to hold, among others, that a layman can be an arahant while remaining a householder and that space is unconditioned.
summary: An unidentified group of northern Indian Buddhists to whom the Kathāvatthu commentary attributes several refuted views.
notes: Identity unknown; reported by an opponent only. Created by U37.

name: Vetulyakas (as named in the Kathāvatthu commentary and Sri Lankan chronicles)
distinctive_positions: Reported (by the Kathāvatthu commentary) to hold that the Buddha did not really live in the human world and did not himself teach the Dhamma (a created form taught it), and that the Saṅgha does not really accept offerings.
summary: A group whose 'Vetulya' teachings were rejected by the Mahāvihāra; the chronicles report their suppression by Sri Lankan kings; the commentary calls them Mahāsuññatāvādins.
notes: Reported by opponents only; identification with any Mahāyāna school is a scholarly hypothesis and is not made here. Created by U37.
